title: This email could've been a meeting
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Shaun Brien, a Victorian school leader, responds to a new state agreement that halves compulsory teacher meetings from 80 hours to 40 hours a year. He admits he actually values well-run meetings and worries the change gives the illusion of returning time to teachers while the underlying workload is unchanged. His second concern is that fewer, more contested staff meetings will make it harder to sustain whole-school initiatives such as the science of learning and explicit teaching. Rather than lament the cap, he proposes four planning questions: how long meetings need to run, what each is for, whether needs change across the year, and whether timetabling can fit collaboration into the school day. The piece is practical and candid, grounded in his own experience of 45-minute versus 60-minute meetings. It treats meeting design as a culture issue, since padded agendas and information-delivery sessions erode staff goodwill.
points: Cutting meeting hours does not cut the work, so collaboration, moderation and task delegation shift onto teachers' self-directed time and favour those who dodge shared responsibility.
Time pressure can help: Brien found 45-minute meetings produced faster action than hour-long ones, so meeting length should be set by agenda rather than habit.
A meeting that could have been an email should be an email, with leaders holding staff accountable for reading it and planning agendas a term ahead to give psychological safety.
With only about 40 hours a year, schools can schedule meetings seasonally, skipping exam weeks and front-loading initiative work early in the year.
Creative timetabling, such as using exam periods or splitting staff across assembly supervision, can fit collaboration into the school day.
quotes: My greatest frustration is a meeting where a staff member can passively sit and exist for what is usually one whole hour without a single thought running through their mind. Presence without purpose.
My first concern with this change specifically goes towards teachers and their workload. Despite the illusion of giving time back to staff, their workload hasn’t changed at all.
Oddly, when all meetings are an hour long we become very good at making meetings last for an hour with no conscious thought to whether or not they need to be.

Staff can very quickly see when agenda items are being added to pad for time or when information is simply being delivered to run out the clock. It is an incredibly fast way to erode any positive culture and good faith which has been built up with your team.

In terms of creating meetings with purpose, I would suggest ensuring that any meeting which could’ve been an email is actually an email and we lift the expectation around the accountability for staff that they are reading those emails.

It’ll mean schools can opt to run no meetings in exam weeks to give staff more time for assessing and reporting and then running more meetings early in the year when implementing and refining new initiatives within the school.
Meetings need to create the momentum needed for change and to improve the knowledge of teachers which they can then put into practice in the classroom.
